mainTopic: The end of the משנה on the wife's oath; the Jerusalem decree-judges; and how judges may and may not take money from the people in a case
overview: The amud opens with the end of the משנה. חנן says a wife whose husband went overseas swears only at the end, when she collects her כתובה. The בני כהנים גדולים, joined by רבי דוסא בן הרכינס, say she swears at the beginning too, and רבן יוחנן בן זכאי sides with חנן. The גמרא then asks about the Jerusalem judges. Some sources list them differently, and one calls them judges of 'thefts' instead of 'decrees.' The גמרא answers that they made decrees about theft cases, and that ירושלים had hundreds of courts but only a few decree-makers, who were paid from Temple funds. Next comes the judge קרנא, who took a small coin from both sides. Step by step, the גמרא shows this was neither שוחד nor pay for judging. It was pay for obvious lost work time, like רב הונא asking for a worker to replace him. The amud ends with teachings on how bribes blind judges, even great sages, and that explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: חנן: the wife swears only at the end
steps.stepSummary: חנן rules that the wife takes a שבועה when she collects her כתובה at the end, not when she starts receiving מזונות.
steps.simpleTranslation: She takes an oath at the end, and she does not take an oath at the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: We are in the middle of the משנה, reading חנן's ruling about a woman whose husband went overseas.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the 'beginning', soon after he leaves, she asks the court for מזונות (food and support). At the 'end', when she hears he died, she collects her כתובה. חנן says she only swears at the end, that her husband left her nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: At the end (when collecting the כתובה)
At the beginning (when asking for מזונות)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Beginning' and 'end' are not the start and end of the marriage itself. They refer to the start of his trip overseas and the time she learns he died.

phrases.english: She takes an oath at the end,
phrases.notes: The 'end' is when she hears her husband died and comes to collect her כתובה.

phrases.english: and she does not take an oath at the beginning.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to חנן, the wife swears only when she collects her כתובה, not when she receives מזונות.

steps.title: The sons of the High Priests: she swears at both times
steps.stepSummary: The בני כהנים גדולים disagree and require a שבועה both at the beginning and at the end. רבי דוסא בן הרכינס agrees with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The sons of the High Priests disagreed with him and said: She swears at the beginning and at the end. רבי דוסא בן הרכינס said: The law follows their words.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings the other side: the בני כהנים גדולים want an oath at both stages, and רבי דוסא בן הרכינס sides with them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In their view, even the early collection of מזונות needs an oath. She must swear that her husband did not leave her money for her support.

phrases.english: The sons of the High Priests disagreed with him,
and said: She takes an oath at the beginning and at the end.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי דּוֹסָא בֶּן הַרְכִּינָס כְּדִבְרֵיהֶם.
phrases.english: Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas said: The law is like their words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing opinion to חנן's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wife swears both when she collects מזונות and when she collects her כתובה. רבי דוסא בן הרכינס agrees.

steps.title: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי sides with חנן
steps.stepSummary: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי approves of חנן's view: she swears only at the end.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי said: חנן spoke well. She takes an oath only at the end.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה closes with רבן יוחנן בן זכאי backing חנן's opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After רבי דוסא sided with the בני כהנים גדולים, רבן יוחנן בן זכאי pushes back. He says חנן was right: there is no oath when she receives מזונות.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two sides. חנן and רבן יוחנן בן זכאי say she swears only at the end. The בני כהנים גדולים and רבי דוסא say she swears at both times.

phrases.english: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai said:
Ḥanan spoke well,
she takes an oath only at the end.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי דוסא by supporting חנן.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי rules like חנן: the oath is only at the end.

steps.title: A ברייתא contradicts the משנה about the Jerusalem judges
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists three judges of 'thefts' in ירושלים. The משנה mentioned only two judges of 'decrees'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a contradiction was raised: There were three judges of theft cases in ירושלים: אדמון בן גדאי, חנן המצרי, and חנן בן אבישלום. The 'three' contradicts the 'two', and 'thefts' contradicts 'decrees'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins. It sets a ברייתא against the משנה's earlier statement that two judges of decrees (אדמון and חנן) were in ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two problems. First, the number: the ברייתא says three judges, but the משנה named two. Second, their title: the ברייתא calls them judges of גזילות (thefts), while the משנה calls them judges of גזירות (decrees).

keyTerms.meaning: And they set a contradiction against it

steps.confusionAlert: גזירות (decrees) and גזילות (thefts) sound almost the same. Read them slowly, because the whole question depends on the difference.

phrases.english: GEMARA: And they raised a contradiction:
There were three judges of theft cases in Jerusalem:
Admon ben Gaddai, and Ḥanan the Egyptian,
and Ḥanan ben Avishalom.
Three against two is difficult,
phrases.notes: The משנה named only two judges who made decrees in ירושלים.

phrases.english: decrees against thefts is difficult!

steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's earlier description of 'two judges of decrees in ירושלים'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא gives a different number of judges and a different title for them.

steps.title: The number is not a problem, but the title still is
steps.stepSummary: The תנא of the משנה mentioned only the judges who mattered to him. That answers the number. The decrees/thefts problem still stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, three against two is not difficult: the ones that mattered to him he taught, and the one that did not matter to him he did not teach. But decrees against thefts is difficult!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the first problem and then repeats that the second problem is still open. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving someone out does not deny that he existed. The משנה only named the judges whose rulings it was quoting. The difference between 'decrees' and 'thefts' is a real wording conflict, so it still needs an answer.

phrases.english: Granted, three against two is not difficult:
those that were important to him, he teaches,
phrases.notes: 'Him' means the תנא of the משנה, who only listed the judges relevant to his topic.

phrases.english: those that were not important to him, he does not teach.
But decrees against thefts is difficult!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles half of the question and sharpens the other half.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Selective listing: the משנה names only the judges relevant to its topic.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two judges versus three seemed to be a factual contradiction.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה simply did not list everyone. The decrees/thefts problem remains.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק: they made decrees about thefts
steps.stepSummary: Both titles are correct: these judges issued decrees on matters of theft and damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: They would issue decrees about thefts.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers the remaining problem by combining the two descriptions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source needs to be changed. The judges are 'decree makers' because they set fixed rulings, and those rulings dealt with theft and damage cases. So the משנה and the ברייתא each describe a different side of the same people.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
That they would issue decrees about thefts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem left open in the previous step.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Harmonization: both titles fit the same judges.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Judges of decrees' and 'judges of thefts' seemed to be two different jobs.
steps.terutzMaskana: They made decrees in theft and damage cases, so both titles are accurate.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how the גמרא can solve a contradiction by showing that both sources are true, without rejecting either one.

steps.title: Example: fixed payments for a damaged young plant
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes the Jerusalem decree-makers setting fixed payments for a young plant that an animal chewed off.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: If an animal cut off a young plant, רבי יוסי says: The decree-makers in Jerusalem say: For a one-year-old plant, two silver coins; for a two-year-old plant, four silver coins.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports רב נחמן בר יצחק with a ברייתא that shows the Jerusalem judges issuing a decree about a damages case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the 'decree makers' fixed a set payment for property damage instead of judging each case separately. That is a decree about a theft-and-damages case, exactly as רב נחמן בר יצחק said.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא

steps.whatToRemember: The judges of ירושלים were called 'decree makers' because they set fixed rulings in theft and damage cases, such as a set payment for a damaged young plant.

phrases.english: As it was taught: If it cut off a young plant,
phrases.notes: 'It' is an animal that chewed off a young plant in someone else's field.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
The decree-makers who were in Jerusalem say:
A plant one year old: two silver coins,
two years old: four silver coins.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up רב נחמן בר יצחק's answer with an example.
steps.raayaObject: That the Jerusalem judges issued decrees about damage and theft cases.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא quoting רבי יוסי about fixed payments for a young plant an animal destroyed.

steps.title: Another ברייתא lists נחום as a third decree-judge
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא names three decree-judges in ירושלים: אדמון, חנן, and נחום. That clashes with the earlier sources, which do not list נחום.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised a contradiction: There were three judges of decrees in ירושלים: אדמון, חנן, and נחום!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different ברייתא that lists three decree-judges, and one of them is נחום. This does not fit the earlier sources, which never mention him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 explained why the משנה named only two judges. The problem now is not the number but the name: this ברייתא adds נחום, while the earlier sources do not list him. So which list is right?

keyTerms.meaning: And they raised a contradiction (one source is set against another)
נחום, the extra judge named in this ברייתא

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
There were three judges of decrees in Jerusalem:
Admon, Ḥanan, and Naḥum!
phrases.notes: The earlier sources did not include נחום. That is the whole problem here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets a new ברייתא against the earlier list of judges
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier sources' list of the decree-judges
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another ברייתא includes נחום, and the earlier sources do not, so the sources seem to disagree about who the judges were

steps.title: Listing נחום follows רבי נתן's minority view
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the ברייתא that names נחום follows רבי נתן. The חכמים did not agree with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Who taught נחום? It is רבי נתן. As it is taught: רבי נתן says, נחום the Mede was also one of the decree-makers in ירושלים, but the חכמים did not agree with him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא explains that the ברייתא naming נחום reflects the view of רבי נתן, which the חכמים rejected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two lists come from different תנאים. רבי נתן counted נחום among the decree-makers. The חכמים did not accept his view, so the other sources leave him out.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is the תנא who taught this?
And the חכמים did not agree with him

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:

phrases.aramaic: מַאן תְּנָא נַחוּם — רַבִּי נָתָן הִיא.
phrases.english: Who taught Naḥum? It is Rabbi Natan.
As it is taught: Rabbi Natan says:
Naḥum the Mede, too,
was one of the decree-makers in Jerusalem,
but the Sages did not agree with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן תְּנָא נַחוּם — רַבִּי נָתָן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction in Step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different תנאים: the ברייתא follows a minority opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sources seemed to disagree about who the decree-judges were
steps.terutzMaskana: Listing נחום follows רבי נתן. The חכמים disagreed, so the other sources leave him out

steps.title: Weren't there hundreds of courts in ירושלים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how there could be only two or three judges, since ירושלים had 394 courts.
steps.simpleTranslation: And were there no more? But didn't רבי פנחס say in the name of רבי אושעיא: There were 394 courts in ירושלים, with the same number of synagogues, study halls, and schools for children!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea of so few judges by quoting a teaching that ירושלים had 394 courts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If ירושלים had 394 courts, it must have had many judges. So how can the sources speak as if there were only two or three?

phrases.english: And there were no more?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי פִּנְחָס אָמַר רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא:
phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Pineḥas say that Rabbi Oshaya said:
Three hundred and ninety-four
courts there were in Jerusalem,
and the same number of synagogues,
and the same number of study halls,
and the same number of schools for children!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתוּ לֵיכָּא? וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי פִּנְחָס אָמַר רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the small count of judges discussed in Steps 8 and 9
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that ירושלים had only two or three judges
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 394 courts means many judges, not just a handful

steps.title: Many judges, but only a few decree-makers
steps.stepSummary: There were many judges, but the short list counts only those who made decrees.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were many judges. When we speak of a few, we are speaking about the decree-makers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that ירושלים did have many judges. The short list counts only the special judges who made decrees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being a judge and being a decree-maker are not the same thing. Hundreds of courts judged cases, but only a few judges set binding decrees, and only they are being counted.

phrases.english: There were many judges,
and when we say this,
we are saying it about the decree-makers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 10
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The short list seemed to claim there were only a few judges in ירושלים
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the decree-makers were few. Ordinary judges were many
steps.whatToRemember: The two or three named judges were the decree-makers, not the only judges in ירושלים.

steps.title: How the decree-makers were paid
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי says the decree-makers were paid 99 מנה from the Temple funds, and if they did not want that, more was added.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב אסי: The decree-makers in ירושלים took their pay, 99 מנה, from the תרומת הלשכה. If they did not want this, they added to it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about the salary of the decree-makers and where the money came from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their pay came from the public Temple fund, not from the people whose cases they judged. The last phrase, 'if they did not want, they added,' sounds strange, and the גמרא questions it in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A large sum of money (one hundred זוז)
The public fund collected for the Temple

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב אַסִּי:
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav Asi said:
The decree-makers in Jerusalem
would take their pay,
ninety-nine maneh,
from the collection of the Temple chamber.
If they did not want it, they would add to it for them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from who the decree-makers were to how they were paid
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The decree-makers received 99 מנה from תרומת הלשכה, and more could be added

steps.title: Were these judges greedy?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether 'if they did not want' means they demanded more money. That would make them wicked.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If they did not want'? Are we dealing with wicked people?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the wording of רב אסי, because it sounds as if the judges complained and got a raise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read simply, 'if they did not want, they added' means the judges turned down their pay to get more. Great judges would not act out of greed, so the wording cannot mean that.

phrases.english: 'They did not want'?
Are we dealing with wicked people?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of Step 12
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It would describe the judges as greedy, which cannot be true of such judges

steps.title: If it was not enough, they added even against the judges' wishes
steps.stepSummary: The wording is fixed: if the pay was not enough, more was added even though the judges did not want it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: if it was not enough for them, then even though they did not want it, they added to their pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא changes the meaning: the extra money was given because the judges needed it, not because they asked for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now 'they did not want' means the opposite of greed: the judges did not want more money. Still, if their pay did not cover their needs, the community added to it so they could keep serving.

keyTerms.meaning: It was not enough for them

phrases.english: Rather: if it was not enough for them,
even though they did not want it,
they would add to their pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 13 by rereading רב אסי's words
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The judges seemed to refuse their pay to get more
steps.terutzMaskana: If the pay did not cover their needs, more was added even though the judges did not want it
steps.whatToRemember: Communal judges were paid from public funds, and their pay was raised to meet their needs even if they did not ask.

steps.title: קרנא took a coin from each side
steps.stepSummary: The judge קרנא took a small coin from both sides, the innocent and the guilty, and then judged their case.
steps.simpleTranslation: קרנא would take an איסתירא from the innocent side and an איסתירא from the guilty side, and judge their case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about how the judge קרנא took a small payment from both people before judging. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the decree-makers, who were paid from public funds, קרנא took his money straight from the people in the case. He took the same amount from both sides.

keyTerms.meaning: The innocent side, the one who wins
The guilty side, the one who loses

phrases.english: Karna would take
an istera from the innocent side
and an istera from the guilty side,
and he would judge their case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from judges paid by the public to a judge who took money from the people in the case
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קרנא took an equal small coin from both sides before judging

steps.title: Isn't that taking a bribe?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how קרנא could do this, since the תורה says 'Do not take a bribe.'
steps.simpleTranslation: How could he do this? Isn't it written: 'And you shall take no bribe'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges קרנא's practice, because taking money from people in a case looks like שוחד. Step 17 suggests a first answer, which step 18 rejects; steps 19, 21 and 25 then build the answer that holds up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק forbids a judge to take שוחד, and קרנא took money straight from the people in the case. On its face, that looks like what the פסוק forbids. Whether taking the same amount from both sides changes anything is tested in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: A bribe, any money a judge takes from people in a case

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think שוחד means only paying a judge to rule unfairly. Here קרנא took the same coin from both sides, and the גמרא still asks whether it is forbidden.

phrases.english: But how could he do this?
Isn't it written: "And you shall take no bribe"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the practice described in Step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: קרנא's practice of taking a coin from each side
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק forbids a judge to take שוחד, and taking money from the people in a case looks like exactly that

steps.title: Maybe taking from both sides is allowed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the איסור of שוחד only applies when a judge takes from one side. קרנא took from both sides, so he would not tilt the case.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might say: the איסור only applies when the judge does not take from both sides, because then he might lean toward the side that paid him. קרנא took from both, so he would not tilt the judgment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible answer to the question of how קרנא could take money. It uses the words 'if you say' because it is about to test this idea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry behind שוחד seems to be that the judge will favor the one who paid. If both sides pay the same, that worry seems to go away. This answer treats the איסור as only about the danger of a crooked ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (introduces a suggested answer)

phrases.english: And if you say: this applies
only where he does not take from both of them,
since perhaps he will come to tilt the judgment;
but קרנא, since he took from both of them,
will not come to tilt the judgment.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּלָא שָׁקֵיל מִתַּרְוַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Suggests an answer to the challenge in step 16 against קרנא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the איסור
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any taking of money by a judge is forbidden שוחד.
steps.terutzMaskana: Perhaps שוחד is only forbidden when it could tilt the case, which taking from both sides does not do.

steps.title: Bribes are forbidden even when the judge rules correctly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. A ברייתא teaches that שוחד is forbidden even if the judge rules correctly.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it really allowed just because he won't tilt the case? A ברייתא teaches that the פסוק 'Do not take a bribe' would be extra if it only meant not to twist justice, since 'Do not twist judgment' already says that. So it must mean that even a judge who rules correctly may not take a bribe.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on step 17 by quoting a ברייתא. The ברייתא says the תורה forbids a bribe even when the ruling stays correct.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא notices that two פסוקים would say the same thing. 'לֹא תַטֶּה מִשְׁפָּט' already forbids crooked rulings, so 'וְשׁוֹחַד לֹא תִקָּח' must add something more. It forbids the bribe itself, even with a correct ruling. So 'he won't tilt the case' does not make קרנא's payment allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it permitted? (a question that expects 'no')
Why does the פסוק need to say this?

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic rule about judges: taking anything from a party to the case is שוחד, even if the judge would have ruled the same way anyway.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי לָא אָתֵי לְאַצְלוֹיֵי דִּינָא מִי שְׁרֵי?
phrases.english: And if he will not come to tilt the judgment, is it permitted?
But it was taught in a ברייתא: 'And do not take a bribe'
Why does the פסוק need to say this?

phrases.aramaic: אִם לְלַמֵּד שֶׁלֹּא לְזַכּוֹת אֶת הַחַיָּיב
phrases.english: If it is to teach not to clear the guilty
and not to find the innocent guilty,
it already says: 'Do not twist judgment.'

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ לְזַכּוֹת אֶת הַזַּכַּאי וּלְחַיֵּיב אֶת הַחַיָּיב
phrases.english: Rather, even to clear the innocent and find the guilty guilty,
the תורה said: 'And do not take a bribe!'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי לָא אָתֵי לְאַצְלוֹיֵי דִּינָא מִי שְׁרֵי? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggested answer in step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that taking from both sides is allowed because it cannot tilt the case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא proves that שוחד is forbidden even when the ruling is correct, so 'no tilting' is not enough to allow it.

steps.title: קרנא took it as a salary, not a bribe
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the איסור is only on money taken as a bribe. קרנא took the money as a fee for his work.
steps.simpleTranslation: That rule is only when he takes it as a bribe. קרנא took it as a salary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer. קרנא's money was a work fee, not a bribe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer does not limit the איסור of שוחד. Instead it says קרנא's payment was a different kind of payment altogether: a fee for his work, which is not a gift meant to win the judge over.

keyTerms.meaning: In the form of / as a kind of

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּשָׁקֵיל בְּתוֹרַת שׁוֹחַד,
phrases.english: This applies only where he takes it as a bribe;
קרנא took it as a salary.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּשָׁקֵיל בְּתוֹרַת שׁוֹחַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 18 knocked out the first answer, this gives a new way to explain קרנא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: קרנא's coin was a kind of שוחד.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was a work fee, not a bribe.

steps.title: A judge who is paid to judge has void rulings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a salary is allowed. A משנה says that one who takes pay to judge has void rulings.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it allowed to take it as a salary? But we learned in a משנה: one who takes pay to judge, his rulings are void!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges step 19. A משנה shows that taking pay for judging is not allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling it a salary instead of a bribe does not help. The משנה says a paid judge's rulings do not count at all. So the 'salary' answer seems to make things worse, not better.

phrases.english: And as a salary, is it permitted?
But we learned in a משנה: One who takes pay to judge,
his rulings are void!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the salary answer of step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that קרנא took a salary.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה says taking pay to judge makes the rulings void, so a salary cannot be allowed.

steps.title: קרנא took pay only for lost work time
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is talking about pay for the judging itself. קרנא only took pay for the work time he lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: That applies to pay for judging. קרנא took pay for lost work time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows its answer. קרנא was not paid for judging. He was only paid back for the time he could not do his regular work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא separates two kinds of pay. Pay for the judging itself is forbidden and makes the ruling void. Pay that only covers lost income (אגר בטילא) is a different thing, and the משנה is not talking about it.

phrases.english: This applies to pay for judging;
קרנא took pay for lost work time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20 by narrowing what קרנא took.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any pay a judge takes counts as forbidden pay for judging.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only pay for the judging itself is forbidden. Pay for lost work time is different.

steps.title: A ברייתא calls a paid judge ugly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether even pay for lost work time is allowed. A ברייתא says a judge who takes pay is 'ugly,' though his ruling counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is pay for lost work time allowed? But a ברייתא teaches: ugly is the judge who takes pay to judge, but his ruling is a valid ruling!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges step 21 with a ברייתא. This step only quotes the ברייתא; the next steps show which case it must be talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the ruling is valid but the judge is still 'ugly,' meaning he acted improperly. If the ברייתא is about pay for lost time, then even that is frowned upon, and קרנא is still not explained.

keyTerms.meaning: His ruling is a valid ruling

phrases.english: And pay for lost work time, is it permitted?
But it was taught in a ברייתא: Ugly is the judge
who takes pay to judge,
except that his ruling is a valid ruling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the 'lost work time' answer of step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that pay for lost work time is allowed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא calls a paid judge 'ugly' even though his ruling stands; if that means pay for lost time, then it is frowned upon too.

steps.title: The ברייתא cannot mean pay for judging
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the ברייתא is about. It cannot be pay for judging, because then the ruling would be void, not valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say it means pay for judging, would his ruling be valid? But a ברייתא teaches: one who takes pay to judge, his rulings are void!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא works out which kind of pay the 'ugly judge' ברייתא is talking about. It rules out the first choice, pay for judging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the ruling is valid. But pay for judging makes rulings void, as we already saw. So the 'ugly judge' ברייתא cannot be about pay for judging.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the details?

phrases.english: What is the case?
If you say pay for judging, would his ruling be valid?
But it was taught: One who takes pay to judge,
phrases.notes: This is the same rule quoted in step 20.

phrases.english: his rulings are void!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Works out the case in the ברייתא of step 22 to make the challenge stronger.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which kind of pay the 'ugly judge' ברייתא is talking about.

steps.title: So even pay for lost time is called ugly
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא must be about pay for lost work time, and it still calls that judge ugly. So the challenge against קרנא stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it must mean pay for lost work time, and still it teaches: ugly is the judge!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the challenge. The 'ugly judge' ברייתא must be about pay for lost time, so that kind of pay is frowned upon too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since pay for judging is ruled out, the only choice left is pay for lost work time. The ברייתא calls that judge 'ugly,' so קרנא's taking such pay is still a problem. The next step answers this.
steps.whatToRemember: There are three kinds of payment: שוחד is forbidden even with a correct ruling; pay for judging makes rulings void; pay for lost time leaves the ruling valid but the judge is called 'ugly.' The next step explains why קרנא was still allowed.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up 'void' and 'ugly.' 'Void' (בטלין) means the ruling does not count. 'Ugly' (מכוער) means the ruling counts, but the judge did something improper.

phrases.english: Rather, it must mean pay for lost work time,
and yet it teaches: Ugly is the judge!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֲגַר בְּטֵילָא, וְקָתָנֵי: מְכוֹעָר הַדַּיָּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23 and so completes the challenge of step 22 against step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The 'ugly judge' ברייתא is about pay for lost work time, so even that is frowned upon.

steps.title: קרנא's lost work time was obvious
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא that calls such a judge 'ugly' is talking about lost work time that is not obvious. קרנא had a real paid job checking wine, so everyone could see what he was losing.
steps.simpleTranslation: That rule applies only when the lost work time is not obvious. קרנא took pay for lost work time that was obvious. He used to check wine in storehouses, and people paid him a זוז for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge against קרנא. It splits lost work time into two kinds: the kind everyone can see, and the kind nobody can see.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא from Step 22 called a judge 'ugly' for taking pay for lost work time. Now the גמרא limits it to cases where the loss is not obvious. קרנא had a known, paid job checking wine, so it was obvious that he was really losing work.

keyTerms.meaning: lost work time, the earnings a judge gives up while judging
obvious, clear for all to see
checks or smells wine to see whether it is going sour

steps.whatToRemember: A judge may take pay for lost work time when it is plain that he really lost work. The judge called 'ugly' is one whose loss nobody can see.

phrases.english: This applies only to lost work time that is not obvious.
phrases.notes: 'This' means the ברייתא that called the judge 'ugly.'

phrases.english: Karna would take pay for lost work time that was obvious,
since he used to check wine in the storehouse
and they would give him a zuz.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge left standing in Step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the case: obvious lost work time versus lost work time nobody can see
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any pay for lost work time makes a judge 'ugly,' so קרנא was wrong to take it
steps.terutzMaskana: Only pay for lost work time that nobody can see is 'ugly.' קרנא's loss was obvious, so he did nothing wrong

steps.title: רב הונא asked for a worker in his place
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא would ask the people in a case to give him a worker to draw water in his place. Then he would judge. This matches the idea of being paid back for clear, real lost work.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what רב הונא did. When a case came before him, he would tell the people: Give me a man to draw water in my place, and I will judge your case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story about רב הונא. It shows the same practice as קרנא's: a judge being covered for real, visible lost work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא did not take money for judging. He only asked for someone to do his own work while he was busy with the case. His loss was obvious, just like קרנא's, so this supports the answer in Step 25.

keyTerms.meaning: draws water, to water the fields
in my place, instead of me

phrases.english: Like this case of Rav Huna:
when a case would come before him,
he would say to them: Give me a man
who will draw water for me in my place,
and I will judge your case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows a story that matches the answer in Step 25
steps.raayaObject: Covering a judge for obvious lost work time is allowed
steps.raayaSupportSource: What רב הונא did: he asked for a worker to replace him

steps.title: Bribe-takers blind their own eyes
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו says people pay a doctor to heal their eyes and may not even be healed. Yet a judge takes a bribe of even a פרוטה and blinds himself for sure.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: Come and see how blind the eyes of bribe-takers are. A person with sore eyes pays a doctor, and maybe he will be healed, maybe not. But these judges take even a פרוטה's worth and blind their own eyes, as the פסוק says: 'For a bribe blinds those who see.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic: taking bribes. רבי אבהו shows how foolish a judge is to take one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He sets two cases side by side. People spend money to fix their eyes, and even then healing is not sure. A judge who takes a bribe pays nothing and gets blindness for sure, from a tiny sum. The proof is the פסוק that says a bribe blinds.

keyTerms.meaning: worth a פרוטה, the smallest amount of money

phrases.english: Rabbi Abahu said: Come and see
how blind are the eyes
of those who accept bribes.
A person has pain in his eyes,
so he gives money to a doctor,
and maybe he is healed, maybe he is not healed.
Yet they take a peruta's worth
phrases.notes: 'They' are the judges who take bribes.

phrases.english: and blind their own eyes,
as it says: "For a bribe blinds those who see."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: בֹּא וּרְאֵה כַּמָּה סְמוּיוֹת עֵינֵיהֶן שֶׁל מְקַבְּלֵי שׁוֹחַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, bribery, which follows from the talk about judges taking money
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even a tiny bribe surely blinds a judge's judgment

steps.title: A קל וחומר from the פסוק about bribes
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads the פסוק: if a bribe blinds the wise, it surely blinds fools; if it twists the words of the righteous, it surely twists the words of the wicked.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'For a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise.' All the more so it blinds fools. 'And twists the words of the righteous.' All the more so it twists the words of the wicked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that reads the bribery פסוק as a קל וחומר. This sets up the challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא reasons that if bribery can harm even the best people, it surely harms weaker people. This reading sounds simple, but the גמרא will soon ask what it adds.

keyTerms.meaning: all the more so: if it is true in the harder case, it is surely true in the easier one

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״כִּי הַשּׁוֹחַד יְעַוֵּר עֵינֵי חֲכָמִים״,
phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: "For a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise,"
all the more so it blinds fools.
"And twists the words of the righteous,"
all the more so it twists the words of the wicked.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״כִּי הַשּׁוֹחַד יְעַוֵּר עֵינֵי חֲכָמִים״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings another source on bribery that reads a second פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bribe harms the wise and righteous, and all the more so fools and the wicked

steps.title: Fools and wicked people are not judges anyway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא would talk about fools and wicked people. They are not fit to be judges at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are fools and wicked people fit to be judges?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's קל וחומר. The point about fools and the wicked seems pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is warning judges. Fools and wicked people would never be chosen as judges, so a קל וחומר about them teaches nothing. So the ברייתא must mean something else.

keyTerms.meaning: is it really so? (it opens a question that expects 'no')

phrases.aramaic: מִידֵּי טִפְּשִׁים וּרְשָׁעִים בְּנֵי דִינָא נִינְהוּ?
phrases.english: Are fools and wicked people fit to be judges?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִידֵּי טִפְּשִׁים וּרְשָׁעִים בְּנֵי דִינָא נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reading in Step 28
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's קל וחומר about fools and the wicked
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Fools and wicked people never judge, so a warning about bribes blinding them has no use

steps.title: A wise judge who takes bribes will lose his mind
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא. Even a very wise man who takes a bribe will not leave the world without his heart being blinded. Then it starts to explain the second half of the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what it means: 'For a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise.' Even a great sage who takes a bribe will not leave the world without blindness of the heart. 'And twists the words of the righteous'...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the reading of the ברייתא. The פסוק is not about fools at all. It warns what will happen to a wise judge who takes bribes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new reading is about punishment, not a קל וחומר. A wise judge who takes bribes will in the end lose his wisdom and become confused. The גמרא then quotes the second half of the פסוק to explain it the same way, and that explanation continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: blindness of the heart, losing clear thinking

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'blindness of the heart' with physical blindness. Here the גמרא means the judge loses his wisdom and clear thinking.
steps.whatToRemember: Bribery is not only a sin in one case. It slowly ruins even a great sage's mind.

phrases.english: Rather, this is what it means:
"For a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise":
even a great sage who takes a bribe
will not leave the world
without blindness of the heart.
"And twists the words of the righteous":
phrases.notes: The explanation of this half of the פסוק continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 29 by reading the ברייתא a new way
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereads the ברייתא: it is about punishment, not a קל וחומר
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא teaches a קל וחומר about fools and wicked people
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא warns that a wise judge who takes bribes will lose his clear thinking
